Lessons.Title: Share Sandwiches
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: interpret and represent fair sharing when a whole-number collection of sandwiches is divided among a whole-number count of people and the share may be fractional. This 2021 lesson invites drawings and explanations before formal fraction-as-division methods in the lessons that follow; do not require a symbolic quotient as the only correct response.

Warm-up — Which One Doesn't Belong? Sandwiches: the 2021 original shows four different food pictures to invite students' informal observations about sandwiches and sharing. The individual source pictures have distinct third-party attributions and are NOT copied or described as though inspected visually. Instead ask learners to name four familiar sandwich styles and defend differences, then ask how whole sandwiches could be divided fairly among friends. Several coherent observations are acceptable.

Activity 1 — Share Sandwiches (20 minutes): fill the blanks '___ sandwiches are shared equally by ___ people' using TWO DISTINCT numbers chosen from 2, 3, and 5, without repeating a chosen number. Draw or describe equal pieces of the SAME whole so every person gets the same amount, with no sandwich lost or double counted. Include one case where a person gets less than one whole sandwich (2 sandwiches and 5 people) and one where a person gets more than one whole (5 sandwiches and 2 people). The source's six possible distinct-number situations are 2÷3, 3÷2, 2÷5, 5÷2, 3÷5 and 5÷3. Explaining equal shares matters more than a formal fraction notation in this introductory lesson.

Activity 2 — The Same Amount (15 minutes): original Student Facing describes Han's drawing for 2 sandwiches shared by 3 people. One sandwich is cut into two halves for people 1 and 2; the other is cut into halves, with one half for person 3 and the remaining half divided into three equal pieces so each person gets another one-sixth. Every person therefore receives one-half plus one-sixth, equivalent to two-thirds of a sandwich. Reconstruct this solution with equal-unit words or tactile strips, then make a DIFFERENT but fair solution: partition each of the two sandwiches into three equal thirds and allocate one third from each to each person.

Teacher assessment: check that shares are equal areas/amounts relative to each same-sized whole, all food is allocated without gaps or duplication, each learner can justify fairness and more-than/less-than-one cases, and different correct diagrams are accepted. This lesson deliberately does not require students to write division expressions or compute formal fractional quotients before they can participate, though a teacher can connect them during discussion. Physical manipulatives, tactile fraction bars, precise verbal explanations and independent first-party diagrams are acceptable.

Edulytiks-original exit check (NOT the publisher 'How Much?'): four congruent sandwiches are fairly shared by three students. Model two different fair distributions using pieces, drawings, tactile strips or precise words. Each student must get 4/3, or 1 and 1/3, sandwiches: for example give one whole sandwich to each, then cut the last sandwich into equal thirds. Explain why each person receives the same amount and all four sandwiches were used. Teacher checks partition equality, allocation, equivalent forms and reasoning; a scalar '4/3' by itself is incomplete.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fair sharing preserves every whole
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each person receives the same amount of the same kind of whole object, even when each share is fractional.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Divide all congruent whole sandwiches into equal-area portions and distribute without overlap or loss.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two equal sandwiches shared by three people give each person two-thirds of one sandwich.

KeyConcepts.Title: Division can describe an amount below or above one
KeyConcepts.Definition: Sharing more people than whole sandwiches gives less than one each; sharing more sandwiches than people may give more than one.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare number of equal wholes available with number of people; explain the relation with a model before requiring symbols.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two sandwiches among five people gives less than one each; five among two gives more than one each.

KeyConcepts.Title: Different partitions can give equivalent fair shares
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiple geometrically different ways of cutting a sandwich can result in the same amount for each person.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check by recombining equal portions and ensuring the sum of people's shares equals the number of wholes.
KeyConcepts.Example: For 2÷3, two one-third pieces from separate sandwiches equal one-half plus one-sixth.

WorkedExamples.Title: Choose two different source numbers
WorkedExamples.Question: Choose 2 sandwiches and 5 people using 2, 3, 5 once each. Is each share less than one sandwich?
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw two equally sized rectangles and partition each into five equal parts.
Steps: Select 2 for sandwiches and 5 for people, without repeating a number.
Cut each whole into five equal pieces and give each person one piece from EACH sandwich.
Every person receives two one-fifth pieces; compare the share to one whole.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Each receives 2/5 of a sandwich, less than one whole.
WorkedExamples.Check: Five people times two-fifths of one sandwich makes exactly two whole sandwiches.

WorkedExamples.Title: A share larger than a whole
WorkedExamples.Question: Five congruent sandwiches are shared by two people. Show a fair distribution.
WorkedExamples.Method: Give each person two whole sandwiches, then split the last into two equal halves.
Steps: Give two whole sandwiches to each of the two people (four wholes allocated).
Divide the remaining fifth sandwich into two equal halves.
Give one half to each person; verify equal 2-and-a-half-sandwich amounts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Han's two-sandwich solution
WorkedExamples.Question: How can two congruent sandwiches be fairly shared among three people using halves and sixths?
WorkedExamples.Method: Combine one half and one sixth of one whole for each learner.
Steps: Cut sandwich 1 into two equal halves for persons 1 and 2.
Cut sandwich 2 into halves, give one half to person 3 and cut the other half into three equal sixth-of-a-whole pieces.
Give each person one sixth in addition to any half already allocated.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Each person receives 1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3 of a sandwich.
WorkedExamples.Check: Three 2/3 shares sum to two whole sandwiches; equivalent alternative: one third of each sandwich per person.

WorkedExamples.Title: Edulytiks original fair-sharing exit
WorkedExamples.Question: Four congruent sandwiches are shared equally among three people. Model the amount per person.
WorkedExamples.Method: Allocate whole sandwiches fairly and partition the final whole into equal thirds.
Steps: Distribute one whole sandwich to each person using three sandwiches.
Cut the fourth into three equal thirds, one for each person.
Verify that all four sandwiches are allocated and each person has one whole plus one third.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Each receives 1 1/3 (or 4/3) sandwiches, with an explanation and representation.
WorkedExamples.Check: 3 × 4/3 = 4; teacher reviews the equality of portions and completeness of the model.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Giving equal numbers of differently sized pieces
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One large piece and one small piece do not represent equal sandwich amounts.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the same-sized whole and compare equal-area fractions, not merely the number of pieces.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forcing all shares to be whole numbers
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Sharing two sandwiches among five people requires a fractional part.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw the sandwiches cut into congruent smaller parts and check each person's share.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Requiring a formal fraction as the only proof of fair sharing
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original introductory task accepts drawings and fairness explanations before formal fraction naming.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Accept an accurate diagram, manipulatives or verbal/tactile explanation; the quotient is a useful optional check.

SummaryPoints: Fair sharing can produce equal fractional amounts even when the numbers of people and sandwiches differ.
Different diagrams or cutting methods can represent the same equal share, provided all wholes are distributed equally and no part is duplicated.
In this introductory lesson, defend the fairness of the representation instead of treating an isolated fraction as full evidence.
